Elishama
ē-lĭsh'ă-mă
n. (the scribe in whose chamber the roll of Jeremiah was laid up before Jehoiakim burned it; also a prince of Ephraim and a son of David)
From Hebrew 'Elishama', “God hath heard”, from 'El, God, and shama', to hear. Several men bear it: the prince of Ephraim in the wilderness census, a son of David born in Jerusalem, a teaching priest under Jehoshaphat, and the scribe of Jeremiah's day.

Biblical Definition

Elishama the scribe holds a small and terrible place in the thirty-sixth chapter of Jeremiah. Baruch had written the prophet's words on a roll and read them in the temple; Michaiah reported it, and the princes sent for Baruch. The scene is set in Elishama's room: “he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe” (Jer 36:12). They heard it read, were afraid, told Baruch to hide himself and Jeremiah with him, and then made a decision that has an official smell to it — “they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe” (Jer 36:20) and went to the king with a verbal summary. Jehoiakim sent Jehudi to fetch it: “he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber” (Jer 36:21), and read three or four leaves at a time, and the king cut them with a penknife and burned them, and none of them were afraid, nor rent their garments. The word of God was filed in a civil servant's office and then destroyed page by page in a winter brazier. God's answer is the point of the chapter: Jeremiah took another roll, Baruch wrote it again, “and there were added besides unto them many like words”.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Elishama; in sacred history it names a prince of Ephraim in the wilderness, a son of David, and the scribe in whose chamber Jeremiah's roll was laid.

expand to see more

ELISHAMA, n. A Hebrew name signifying God hath heard.

Elishama the son of Ammihud was prince of the children of Ephraim in the wilderness, and grandfather of Joshua.

A son of David born unto him in Jerusalem bore the same name.

Elishama, a priest, was sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the law in the cities of Judah.

Elishama the scribe had a chamber in the king's house, where the roll of Jeremiah was laid up before Jehoiakim burned it.

Key Scripture

Jer 36:12 — "Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes."

Jer 36:20 — "And they went in to the king into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and told all the words in the ears of the king."

Jer 36:21 — "So the king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll: and he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber. And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king."

Jer 36:23 — "And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth."

Modern Corruption

The burning of a scroll is taken as proof that the Bible is a fragile human artifact; the chapter records the burning precisely in order to report that the words were written again, and more added.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 36 is the Bible's own account of an attempt to destroy the Bible, and it is remarkably unbothered. The king had the physical roll and burned it completely; the LORD said take another roll and write in it all the former words, “and there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jer 36:32). The doctrine of preservation the dictionary holds is not a claim that no manuscript was ever lost or burned — many were — but that God has providentially preserved His word through every such attempt, so that what He said remains available to His church. Diocletian burned copies, and there are more today. The 1689 Confession states it: the Scriptures were “by his singular care and providence kept pure in all ages.”

The corruption to name in Elishama himself is quieter and closer to home. He and the princes were afraid when they heard the roll — genuinely alarmed, alarmed enough to warn Baruch to hide. And then they filed it. They summarised the contents for the king rather than putting the text in his hands, they let the roll sit in an office, and when Jehudi came for it they did not stand in the doorway. Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah at least made intercession that the king should not burn it. Being moved by the word and taking no risk for it is the characteristic sin of the respectable, and it is how a document that alarms everybody ends up in a drawer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Elishama' (H476), from 'El (H410), God, and shama' (H8085), to hear; sopher (H5608), a scribe; megillah (H4039), a roll.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Elishama' (H476) — Elishama, “God hath heard”.

Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, and so to obey; the root that indicts the men of Jer 36 who heard and did not.

Hebrew sopher (H5608) — a scribe, a writer, one who counts; the civil-service office of the king's house.

Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, scroll; the form of the book Baruch wrote and Jehoiakim burned.

Hebrew ta'ar has-sopher — the scribe's penknife; the tool for trimming reeds, turned into an instrument against the word.

Usage

"“All the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe” — the room where the roll was heard."

"“They laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama” — the word filed rather than obeyed."

"“He cut it with the penknife” — a king's answer to what he had heard."
